column1: # The examples that are expected not to work.
# A pitfall article shows what a mistake looks like, and sometimes that
# means the program crashes. Those files are listed here, and the checker
# expects them to fail instead of reporting them.
# The second column says what the failure is expected to look like, so that
# a file that starts failing in a different way is still reported. The
# third column says in which run the failure is expected: "any" for a
# program that dies on its own, and "sanitizer" for one that only the
# address sanitizer can catch -- reading freed memory usually does not
# crash, it just reads what used to be there.
# The example hands out a reference to a string that is already gone, and
# then reads it. The program dies with a segmentation fault, which is the
# point the article makes.
pitfalls/en/dangling-pointer.md
pitfalls/中文版/悬垂指针.md
# The example reads an iterator that an insert has already invalidated.
# It usually works, because the freed memory still holds the old value,
# and the sanitizer finds the use after free that the article is about.
